item.title: Your Teams Meeting Is Labelled. Are Its Recordings and Notes?
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID: 581739 We spend a lot of time talking about protecting documents, emails and SharePoint sites with Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels. But what happens when that information is discussed in a Teams meeting? A meeting might be labelled Confidential, yet the recording, transcript and meeting notes become separate files stored in SharePoint […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID: 581739

We spend a lot of time talking about protecting documents, emails and SharePoint sites with Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels. But what happens when that information is discussed in a Teams meeting?

A meeting might be labelled Confidential, yet the recording, transcript and meeting notes become separate files stored in SharePoint or OneDrive. If those files aren’t protected consistently, you can end up with a gap in your information protection strategy.

Microsoft is addressing this with sensitivity label inheritance for Teams meeting artifacts.

What’s changing?

Microsoft Purview Roadmap item 581739 introduces the ability for Teams meeting artifacts to inherit the sensitivity label applied to the meeting.

The artifacts include:

  • Recordings – MP4 files.
  • Transcripts – associated with the meeting recording.
  • Meeting notes – Loop files.

When configured, these artifacts automatically receive the meeting’s sensitivity label when they are saved to SharePoint or OneDrive.

The aim is simple: reduce reliance on users remembering to classify every piece of content created during a meeting.

Why does this matter?

Think about a meeting labelled Highly Confidential.

The discussion covers a sensitive acquisition, financial results or an upcoming organisational restructure. The meeting is appropriately classified, but the recording and transcript contain the same sensitive information.

Without consistent labelling, those files could be treated differently from the meeting itself.

Automatic inheritance helps close that gap by carrying the meeting’s classification into the content generated from it.

This is particularly important as organisations use Teams recordings, transcripts, intelligent recap and AI-powered meeting experiences more frequently.

How does it work?

The administrator configures the Apply meeting label to artifacts option in the Microsoft Purview sensitivity label publishing policy.

When enabled, the meeting’s sensitivity label is applied to supported recordings, transcripts and Loop meeting notes as they are saved to SharePoint or OneDrive.

There are a few important implementation details:

  1. MP4 support matters. Sensitivity labelling support for MP4 files must be enabled for recordings and transcripts to receive the label. If it isn’t enabled, selecting the policy option won’t label those files.
  2. It’s applied when the artifact is saved. If someone changes the meeting’s sensitivity label afterwards, the existing artifacts do not automatically inherit that new label.
  3. Encryption has consequences. Recordings and transcripts with an encryption-enabled label can be played in supported browser experiences, but cannot be downloaded. Where the label doesn’t apply encryption, a downloaded copy does not retain the sensitivity label.
  4. Publishing matters. The relevant sensitivity labels must be published to meeting organisers and participants.

These details are important when designing the experience. Automatic labelling is useful, but it needs to align with how people access, share and retain meeting content.

What should administrators do?

I’d approach this in five steps:

1. Review your sensitivity label strategy

Make sure your labels represent meaningful business classifications. Avoid creating a complicated taxonomy that users cannot understand.

2. Review meeting label publishing policies

Decide which users can apply labels to meetings and whether a default meeting label or mandatory labelling is appropriate.

3. Enable artifact inheritance

Configure the Apply meeting label to artifacts setting in the relevant publishing policy.

4. Validate MP4 support and encryption

Test recordings, transcripts and Loop notes. Confirm that the resulting files receive the expected label and that encryption behaves as intended.

5. Test the end-to-end experience

Check access, sharing, playback, downloads and retention. In particular, test what happens when the meeting label changes after the artifacts have been created.

A roadmap detail worth noting

Roadmap ID 581739 is currently listed as In development, with General Availability targeted for December 2026. Its listed cloud environments are GCC, GCC High and DoD.

There is an important distinction for commercial tenants: Microsoft previously listed the same capability under roadmap ID 558686, which was marked Launched for Worldwide commercial tenants. So don’t assume 581739 represents a brand-new commercial rollout. Check the existing capability and your tenant’s availability.

The Jim Talks takeaway:

Sensitivity labels shouldn’t stop at the meeting invitation.

The information discussed in a meeting can become a recording, transcript, Loop note or AI-generated recap. Those artifacts may contain exactly the same sensitive information as the original conversation.

The governance principle is simple: protection should follow the information, not depend on someone remembering to apply it again.

As organisations increasingly rely on AI to capture, summarise and act on meetings, consistent classification becomes even more important.

Don’t just label the meeting. Think about everything the meeting creates.

References

  • Microsoft 365 Roadmap – ID 581739
  • Microsoft 365 Roadmap – ID 558686
  • Microsoft Learn – Use sensitivity labels to protect calendar items, Teams meetings, and chat

Roadmap status and dates checked 21 November 2026.

item.title: 🔥 5 Microsoft Purview Controls Every Organisation Should Review Before Deploying AI Agents
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: AI agents are moving beyond answering questions. They’re searching SharePoint, summarising documents, retrieving customer information, interacting with business applications, calling APIs and, increasingly, taking actions on behalf of employees. That creates a very different data governance challenge. A traditional application might allow an employee to open a document. An AI agent could potentially retrieve information […]
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are moving beyond answering questions. They’re searching SharePoint, summarising documents, retrieving customer information, interacting with business applications, calling APIs and, increasingly, taking actions on behalf of employees.

That creates a very different data governance challenge.

A traditional application might allow an employee to open a document. An AI agent could potentially retrieve information from multiple documents, combine it, summarise it and send the result somewhere else.

The agent might be working exactly as designed. The problem could be that the underlying data is overshared, insufficiently classified or not adequately protected.

AI agents don’t remove existing information governance problems, they can amplify them.

Before deploying agents into your organisation, I recommend reviewing these five Microsoft Purview control areas.

1. Data Security Posture Management (DSPM): Know what your agents can see

You cannot govern what you cannot see.

Before deploying agents, establish where sensitive information exists, where it is exposed and how AI is interacting with organisational data.

Microsoft Purview Data Security Posture Management (DSPM), including its AI-related capabilities, can help organisations understand data exposure and AI usage.

Review:

  • Where sensitive information is stored across Microsoft 365.
  • Whether SharePoint sites and OneDrive content are overshared.
  • Whether sensitive information is appropriately classified and labelled.
  • Which supported AI applications and agents are being used.
  • Whether AI interactions are exposing sensitive information.
  • Which recommended remediation actions should be prioritised.

Pay particular attention to inherited permissions, broad access groups, stale content and documents that have never been classified.

Imagine an agent designed to help HR employees answer policy questions. If its users have access to an old SharePoint site containing confidential employee information, the agent may be able to retrieve that information too.

The agent isn’t necessarily the problem. The data access model is.

Jim’s takeaway: Assess your information estate before connecting agents to it. Fix oversharing and data exposure before expanding AI access.

2. Sensitivity Labels and Information Protection: Give your data context

An AI agent needs more than permission to access information. Your organisation needs to understand the sensitivity of that information and apply the appropriate protection.

Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels help classify and protect organisational information.

Before deploying agents, review:

  • Your sensitivity label taxonomy.
  • Whether labels are consistently applied to important information.
  • Whether appropriate encryption and access restrictions are configured.
  • Whether labels are available to the supported AI workloads.
  • Whether your policies restrict agents from processing particular sensitive content.

For example, you might have labels such as:

  • Public
  • General
  • Confidential
  • Highly Confidential

A document labelled Highly Confidential may require stronger controls than a document labelled General.

For supported Copilot Studio scenarios, Purview can use sensitivity labels to restrict processing of protected SharePoint knowledge sources through applicable DLP policies. Sensitivity label support also varies by agent type and knowledge source.

Do not assume that applying a sensitivity label automatically blocks every AI agent from accessing the content. The label, encryption, user permissions, agent type and applicable policy configuration all matter.

Jim’s takeaway: Your labels need to mean something operationally. A classification scheme that is inconsistently applied or not connected to enforcement policies provides limited protection.

3. Data Loss Prevention (DLP): Control what agents can process and share

This is one of the most important controls to review before introducing autonomous or semi-autonomous agents.

An agent may retrieve information from one system and use it in another. It might send an email, create a Teams message, update a record or pass information to an external service.

You need to understand where DLP can inspect and restrict those activities.

Review:

  • Which AI application locations are covered by your DLP policies.
  • Whether sensitive information in prompts and responses is detected.
  • Whether labelled content can be restricted from supported agent interactions.
  • Whether external sharing and communication actions are controlled.
  • Whether endpoint DLP protects users interacting with third-party AI services.
  • Whether custom connectors, HTTP actions and external integrations have been assessed separately.

For example, consider an agent that can retrieve customer information from SharePoint and send an email.

You should establish whether the relevant Purview DLP policies can detect and restrict sensitive information in the supported interaction and communication paths.

For Copilot Studio agents, Microsoft documents specific DLP and sensitivity-label support, including restrictions for supported SharePoint knowledge-source scenarios. Do not assume every agent action or external connector is automatically inspected by Purview DLP.

Jim’s takeaway: Don’t just ask what data an agent can read. Ask where that data can go next, and which controls can prevent it from leaving an approved boundary.

4. Insider Risk Management: Detect risky AI behaviour

Not every AI-related incident starts with a malicious employee.

An employee might accidentally provide sensitive information in a prompt. An agent might be manipulated through prompt injection. Someone might attempt to use AI to access or extract information they should not be handling.

Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management (IRM) can help identify and investigate supported risky AI usage.

Review:

  • Whether the Risky AI Usage policy template is configured.
  • Whether relevant AI activities are being monitored.
  • Whether prompt injection and attempts to access protected materials are included in your risk assessment.
  • Whether investigation teams have appropriate permissions.
  • Whether privacy controls, including pseudonymisation, are configured.
  • Whether alerts can be investigated and escalated through your existing security processes.

The objective is not to treat every unusual AI interaction as misconduct.

It is to identify activity that may indicate data theft, inappropriate use or an attempt to bypass organisational controls.

For example, an employee repeatedly attempting to use an agent to retrieve restricted information may warrant investigation, particularly when combined with other relevant risk indicators.

Jim’s takeaway: AI governance needs to consider user behaviour as well as agent behaviour. You need visibility into how people are using agents, not simply whether an agent has been deployed.

5. Audit, Retention and eDiscovery: Know what happened and preserve the evidence

If an AI agent accesses sensitive information, produces an unexpected response or takes an inappropriate action, can your organisation establish what happened?

This is where audit and compliance controls become essential.

Review:

  • Whether supported agent interactions are captured in the unified audit log.
  • Whether prompts, responses and relevant activity records are available.
  • Whether the records provide sufficient context for an investigation.
  • Whether retention policies cover the relevant AI interaction data.
  • Whether eDiscovery teams can search, review and preserve relevant evidence.
  • Whether communication compliance policies are appropriate for supported AI interactions.

Microsoft Purview Audit can capture supported AI activity, including prompts and responses, depending on the application and integration.

Data Lifecycle Management can help manage the retention and deletion of supported AI interaction data. eDiscovery can support the preservation, collection and review of relevant information where supported.

This is particularly important for regulated organisations.

You should be able to answer questions such as:

  • Which user or agent initiated the interaction?
  • What information was accessed?
  • What was generated?
  • When did the activity happen?
  • What evidence is available?
  • How long must the relevant records be retained?

Remember that logging an interaction is not the same as retaining every piece of source data or recording every action taken by an external system. Validate the actual audit coverage for each agent platform.

Jim’s takeaway: If you cannot reconstruct what an agent did, you will struggle to investigate incidents, demonstrate compliance or establish accountability.

The important point: Purview coverage is not identical for every agent

These controls are not a universal switch that protects every AI agent.

Microsoft publishes capability and application-specific guidance for Microsoft 365 Copilot agents, Copilot Studio agents, Agent 365 and other supported AI applications.

For example, Microsoft’s Copilot Studio guidance identifies support for DSPM, auditing, data classification and sensitivity labels, with specific DLP and Insider Risk Management capabilities. Some scenarios also require pay-as-you-go billing, particularly for agents published to non-Microsoft channels.

Before deployment, validate:

  1. Which agent platform you are using.
  2. Where the agent is published.
  3. Which knowledge sources it accesses.
  4. Which connectors and tools it can call.
  5. Which Purview capabilities are supported for that exact scenario.
  6. Whether additional licensing, billing or configuration is required.

Also remember that Purview is one part of the governance model. It does not replace Microsoft Entra identity controls, least-privilege permissions, agent ownership, connector governance, secure development or operational monitoring.

My recommended pre-deployment checklist

Before an agent is approved for production, I would want evidence that these five areas have been reviewed.

  • DSPM: Sensitive data exposure and AI usage assessed.
  • Information Protection: Sensitivity labels and protection policies reviewed.
  • DLP: Supported agent interactions and data movement protected.
  • Insider Risk Management: Risky AI usage detection and investigation considered.
  • Audit and compliance: Logging, retention and eDiscovery requirements validated.

I would also require an identified business owner, a technical owner, approved knowledge sources, documented permissions and a process to disable the agent if something goes wrong.

The Jim Talks takeaway:

Organisations are rightly excited about what AI agents can do. But giving an agent access to business information is not simply another application deployment.

It introduces a new way for information to be discovered, combined, processed and acted upon.

We have spent years building governance around what employees can access and what they can share. Now we need to apply those principles to what agents can access and what they can do with it.

My framework remains:

DATA → IDENTITY → AGENT → TOOLS → ACTION → OUTCOME

Microsoft Purview plays a critical role in governing the data and compliance aspects of that journey.

But the real objective is not to deploy more controls. It is to make sure that when an AI agent is given the ability to act, the organisation understands the data it can reach, the boundaries it must respect and the evidence it leaves behind.

Don’t deploy the agent first and work out the governance afterwards. Make governance part of the deployment decision.

Microsoft resources

  • Microsoft Purview – Data security and compliance for AI agents
  • Microsoft Purview – Copilot Studio agent security and compliance
  • Microsoft Purview – Protect sensitive data to get ready for AI
  • Microsoft Purview – Data security and compliance for generative AI apps
  • Microsoft Purview – Insider Risk Management
  • Microsoft Purview – Audit

Always validate current licensing, feature availability and supported agent scenarios against Microsoft’s documentation before implementing controls.

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575284: Retention Doesn’t Have to Mean Keeping Every File Version Forever
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: If you manage Microsoft 365, particularly SharePoint Online and OneDrive, you’ll probably be familiar with the storage challenges that come with document version history. Versioning is incredibly useful. It allows users to recover previous versions of documents, investigate changes and restore content when something goes wrong. But there’s another side to it. In organisations with […]
item.content:encoded:
If you manage Microsoft 365, particularly SharePoint Online and OneDrive, you’ll probably be familiar with the storage challenges that come with document version history.

Versioning is incredibly useful. It allows users to recover previous versions of documents, investigate changes and restore content when something goes wrong.

But there’s another side to it.

In organisations with large SharePoint environments, heavily edited documents can accumulate significant numbers of versions. Multiply that across thousands of sites, libraries and users, and the storage footprint can become substantial.

Now add Microsoft Purview retention policies into the equation.

Historically, content subject to a retention policy or eDiscovery hold has been protected from normal SharePoint version history limits. This is important from a compliance perspective, but it can also mean that version storage grows beyond the limits administrators would normally expect.

Microsoft roadmap item 575284 is looking to address this.

What is Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575284?

The roadmap item is titled:

Microsoft Purview: Data Lifecycle Management – Enable version trimming for data covered by retention policies in OneDrive and SharePoint.

The planned capability will allow administrators with the appropriate Purview permissions to enable version cleanup for SharePoint and OneDrive content, even when retention policies are in effect.

The intention is to allow SharePoint version management to trim file versions according to configured limits, while maintaining the necessary protections for specific content that must be preserved.

In other words, Microsoft is looking to give organisations more control over the storage impact of version history without simply removing their retention controls.

Roadmap details:

  • Roadmap ID: 575284
  • Product: Microsoft Purview – Data Lifecycle Management
  • Status: In development
  • Planned preview: November 2026
  • Planned rollout: January 2027
  • Platform: Web

These are planned dates, not guaranteed delivery dates. Check the roadmap for the latest status before making deployment plans.

Why does this matter?

Let’s consider a practical example.

Imagine an organisation with 20,000 SharePoint sites and several million documents.

A particular Finance document might be updated dozens of times each month. Each update creates another version.

Under normal circumstances, SharePoint version history settings help control how many versions are retained.

However, if that document is subject to a retention policy, the normal version history limits may not apply in the same way.

This is intentional. Microsoft needs to ensure that retention and eDiscovery obligations are honoured.

But consider the consequences:

  • More versions are retained than administrators anticipated.
  • Storage consumption increases.
  • Administrators have less flexibility when managing version history.
  • Storage planning becomes more complicated.
  • Organisations may struggle to balance recovery requirements, compliance and storage costs.

Roadmap 575284 is intended to give administrators another option.

What could administrators do with this?

The most interesting aspect is the potential to bring version management and retention management closer together.

Here are three areas where I think this could make a difference.

1. Better SharePoint storage management

Organisations could potentially apply more controlled version history limits to content covered by retention policies.

This could help reduce unnecessary version accumulation and improve storage management across large SharePoint and OneDrive estates.

However, don’t assume this means every historical version can be deleted. Specific protected cases will continue to require preservation.

2. More flexibility for retention policies

Retention policies exist to meet business, regulatory and legal requirements.

They aren’t necessarily designed to retain every intermediate version of every document indefinitely.

There is an important distinction between retaining the information an organisation is obligated to preserve and retaining every historical version generated during normal document collaboration.

This roadmap item is interesting because it recognises that distinction.

3. Better alignment between compliance and operational requirements

Historically, administrators have often had to consider retention and version management as separate concerns.

This capability could provide more flexibility to manage both together.

For example, an organisation might want to preserve information for seven years while applying sensible version history limits to reduce unnecessary storage consumption.

The important thing will be understanding exactly which versions remain protected and how the new behaviour interacts with retention policies, eDiscovery holds and records.

What should you be doing now?

Although the feature is still in development, there are several things I’d recommend reviewing before it arrives.

1. Understand your current version storage

Look at your SharePoint and OneDrive storage consumption.

Identify sites and libraries where version history is contributing significantly to storage usage.

Don’t assume the largest sites are necessarily the biggest contributors. A smaller library containing frequently updated documents can accumulate substantial version history.

2. Review your version history settings

Understand the version limits currently applied at tenant, site and library level.

Remember that SharePoint supports different configuration levels, and individual sites or libraries can have settings that differ from the organisation defaults.

3. Review retention policies and eDiscovery holds

Identify which SharePoint sites and OneDrive accounts are covered by retention policies or eDiscovery holds.

Understand why the content is being retained and whether the organisation has documented requirements around historical versions.

4. Identify records and regulated content

Pay particular attention to records management requirements.

A document declared as a record has additional protection considerations. Do not assume that version trimming will treat records in the same way as ordinary documents.

5. Establish a governance position

Before enabling any version trimming capability, agree:

  • Which workloads and sites are in scope?
  • What version history limits are appropriate?
  • Which content must retain historical versions?
  • What recovery requirements apply?
  • Who is authorised to configure and approve changes?
  • How will the impact be assessed and monitored?

I would strongly recommend testing with a representative set of sites before applying any new configuration more broadly.

One important distinction: retention versus version history

This is the part I think administrators need to understand.

Retention and version history solve different problems.

Retention is about ensuring information is preserved for a defined period or according to a particular business or regulatory requirement.

Version history is about maintaining previous iterations of a document so that changes can be reviewed or content can be restored.

They overlap, but they aren’t the same thing.

A retention policy doesn’t automatically mean that every version must be retained forever. Equally, reducing version history doesn’t mean that an organisation can ignore its retention obligations.

Microsoft’s existing documentation explains how SharePoint version trimming interacts with retention policies and eDiscovery holds. It is worth reading before planning any changes.

The Jim Talks takeaway:

I think roadmap 575284 is a welcome development for organisations managing large SharePoint and OneDrive environments.

For years, administrators have had to balance three competing considerations:

  • Protecting information to meet compliance obligations.
  • Maintaining useful document recovery capabilities.
  • Controlling the storage footprint of Microsoft 365.

This update has the potential to give organisations more flexibility in managing that balance.

But the real opportunity isn’t simply deleting old versions to save storage.

It’s being able to make more informed decisions about what needs to be retained, what needs to remain recoverable and what version history can be managed more efficiently.

Good information governance isn’t about keeping everything forever. It’s about retaining the right information, for the right reasons, for the right amount of time.

That’s the conversation I’d be having before enabling this capability.

Further reading

  • Microsoft 365 Roadmap – ID 575284
  • Microsoft Learn – Trim existing versions in SharePoint
  • Microsoft Learn – Version history limits for SharePoint and OneDrive
  • Microsoft Purview – What’s new

Roadmap information checked: 6 November 2026. Feature availability and timelines are subject to change.

item.title: 🤔 Did You Know? Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management Connects to More of Microsoft 365 Than You Might Think
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: When people talk about Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management (IRM), the conversation often focuses on detecting suspicious user activity. Perhaps someone is downloading large volumes of files before leaving the organisation. Maybe sensitive information is being uploaded to an unauthorised cloud service, or a user is attempting to remove or downgrade sensitivity labels. But here’s […]
item.content:encoded:
When people talk about Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management (IRM), the conversation often focuses on detecting suspicious user activity.

Perhaps someone is downloading large volumes of files before leaving the organisation. Maybe sensitive information is being uploaded to an unauthorised cloud service, or a user is attempting to remove or downgrade sensitivity labels.

But here’s something you might not know:

Insider Risk Management doesn’t have to stop at identifying risky behaviour. It can help other Microsoft security controls respond to that risk.

Through integrations with Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Defender, IRM can become part of a much wider data security and identity protection strategy.

Let’s look at some of the connections.

1. Insider Risk Management + Data Loss Prevention (DLP)

This is one of the most interesting integrations.

Microsoft Purview Adaptive Protection connects Insider Risk Management with Data Loss Prevention.

The idea is straightforward:

  • IRM detects potentially risky behaviour.
  • The user is assigned an insider risk level.
  • DLP policies can use that risk level to determine what actions are allowed.

For example, imagine an employee who has submitted their resignation.

Over several days, IRM detects a sequence of potentially concerning activities:

  • Downloading unusually large volumes of files.
  • Accessing sensitive information.
  • Copying files to removable storage.
  • Attempting to upload information to an unauthorised cloud service.

The user may be assigned an elevated insider risk level.

Adaptive Protection can then influence how DLP responds.

For an elevated-risk user, you could configure DLP to block activities such as copying sensitive files to USB, printing, or sharing information externally.

For a user with a lower risk level, the same activities might simply be audited.

The important point: DLP doesn’t necessarily need to apply the same level of restriction to everyone.

It can respond to the risk context provided by Insider Risk Management.

Microsoft reference: Adaptive Protection in DLP

2. Insider Risk Management + Microsoft Entra Conditional Access

Did you know that insider risk can also influence access decisions?

Through Adaptive Protection, Microsoft Entra Conditional Access can use an Insider Risk condition.

This means access decisions can take account of the risk level identified by Purview.

For example:

  • Minor risk: allow access, with visibility and monitoring.
  • Moderate risk: require additional acknowledgement, such as Terms of Use.
  • Elevated risk: block access to selected Microsoft 365 applications or sensitive SharePoint sites.

You can also use Conditional Access application control to restrict downloads from selected cloud applications.

One particularly interesting scenario involves Microsoft 365 Copilot.

If an elevated-risk user is blocked from accessing a sensitive SharePoint site through an appropriate Conditional Access policy, Copilot cannot use that site as a source of information for that user’s responses.

This is an important connection between identity, data access and AI governance.

It is not simply about detecting a risky user. It is about changing what that user can access.

Microsoft reference: Adaptive Protection configuration guide

3. Insider Risk Management + Data Lifecycle Management

Here’s another integration that deserves attention.

Adaptive Protection can work with Data Lifecycle Management to help preserve information deleted by elevated-risk users.

For example, imagine an employee who is leaving the organisation and starts deleting files from SharePoint, OneDrive or Exchange Online.

With the relevant Adaptive Protection configuration, an automatically created retention label policy can preserve content deleted by users assigned an elevated risk level for 120 days.

Why does this matter?

Because detecting suspicious deletion activity is only part of the problem.

You also need to consider whether the information can be recovered or retained for investigation.

This provides another layer of protection when dealing with potential data loss or malicious deletion.

Microsoft currently documents this capability as part of Adaptive Protection, with Data Lifecycle Management integration identified as a preview capability. Check the current service documentation and licensing before planning deployment.

Microsoft reference: Help dynamically mitigate risks with Adaptive Protection

4. Insider Risk Management + Microsoft Defender XDR

IRM isn’t isolated in the Purview portal either.

You can share Insider Risk Management alerts and user risk context with Microsoft Defender XDR.

This allows security operations teams to investigate insider risk alongside other security signals.

For example, a SOC analyst could investigate:

  • An Insider Risk Management alert.
  • A related Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alert.
  • A Data Loss Prevention alert.
  • Other identity or security activity associated with the same user.

Rather than investigating each signal independently, analysts can gain a more joined-up view of the activity.

Insider Risk Management alerts can appear in the Defender incident and alert queues, and analysts can use Advanced Hunting to investigate relevant information.

This is particularly useful for organisations where the SOC works primarily in Microsoft Defender rather than switching between multiple portals.

Microsoft reference: Investigate insider risk threats in the Microsoft Defender portal

5. Insider Risk Management + Communication Compliance

Another useful connection is with Microsoft Purview Communication Compliance.

IRM can share user risk severity information with Communication Compliance, giving investigators additional context when reviewing potential policy violations.

Think about a situation where an employee is sending inappropriate or potentially sensitive communications while also displaying other indicators of risky behaviour.

Communication Compliance can provide insight into the communications, while Insider Risk Management provides additional user-risk context.

This helps investigators understand the wider picture rather than looking at an individual communication in isolation.

There is also an important connection in the other direction: Communication Compliance activity can be used as a triggering event for certain Insider Risk Management policies.

That creates opportunities to connect communication-related concerns with broader insider risk investigations.

Microsoft reference: Share Insider Risk Management data with other solutions

6. Insider Risk Management + Microsoft Sentinel and SIEM platforms

Finally, don’t forget the wider security ecosystem.

IRM alert information can be exported to SIEM and SOAR solutions using the Office 365 Management Activity API.

Microsoft Sentinel also provides an Insider Risk Management data connector.

This means organisations can bring insider risk information into their wider security monitoring and response processes.

If your SOC uses Sentinel, Splunk or another SIEM platform, this is worth investigating.

Microsoft reference: Share Insider Risk Management data with other solutions

Putting it all together

The real value becomes apparent when you look at these integrations as a connected security model.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. DETECT – Insider Risk Management identifies potentially risky user behaviour.
  2. ASSESS – The user is assigned an appropriate insider risk level.
  3. PROTECT – Adaptive Protection influences DLP policies to restrict risky data activities.
  4. CONTROL – Conditional Access can limit access to Microsoft 365 applications or sensitive SharePoint sites.
  5. PRESERVE – Data Lifecycle Management can preserve relevant deleted content under the configured protection scenario.
  6. INVESTIGATE – Defender XDR, Communication Compliance and SIEM integrations provide additional context for security teams.

A few things to remember

There are some important considerations before switching all these integrations on:

  • Licensing matters. Insider Risk Management, Adaptive Protection, DLP and Conditional Access have specific licensing requirements. Check the relevant Microsoft licensing guidance.
  • Adaptive Protection must be configured. These integrations don’t automatically start enforcing controls just because IRM is enabled.
  • Risk levels aren’t alert severity levels. Adaptive Protection uses Minor, Moderate and Elevated risk levels. These are different from the Low, Medium and High alert severity classifications used by IRM.
  • Test before enforcing. Start with audit or simulation modes where supported. Understand the impact before introducing blocking controls.
  • Privacy and governance matter. IRM uses pseudonymisation by default, role-based access controls and audit logs. Make sure your investigation processes are appropriately governed.

The bigger picture

I think this is one of the most interesting aspects of Microsoft Purview.

Insider Risk Management is not just about identifying employees who might be putting information at risk.

It can help connect the dots between user behaviour, data protection, identity controls, retention and security operations.

Instead of treating DLP, Conditional Access, Defender and Insider Risk Management as separate products, organisations can start using them as connected parts of a broader security strategy.

The Jim Talks takeaway:

Detecting insider risk is important. Using that risk context to adapt your protection is where things get really interesting. Did you know how many Microsoft 365 security capabilities can connect to Insider Risk Management?

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview Roadmap 577187: Read-Only Device Onboarding Access Is Coming
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview is continuing to improve how organisations delegate administrative responsibilities without compromising security. Roadmap ID 577187 introduces a new View-Only Device Management role for the device onboarding experience in Microsoft Purview Endpoint Data Loss Prevention (Endpoint DLP). For organisations working towards least-privilege administration, this is a small but meaningful change. The principle is simple: […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview is continuing to improve how organisations delegate administrative responsibilities without compromising security. Roadmap ID 577187 introduces a new View-Only Device Management role for the device onboarding experience in Microsoft Purview Endpoint Data Loss Prevention (Endpoint DLP).

For organisations working towards least-privilege administration, this is a small but meaningful change.

The principle is simple: people who need visibility into device onboarding should not automatically need permission to manage it.

What is Microsoft introducing?

According to the roadmap entry, Microsoft is developing a more granular approach to access the Devices page under:

Microsoft Purview → Settings → Device Onboarding

Previously, access to device onboarding and management has relied on broader administrative roles, depending on the operation being performed. These can include roles such as Compliance Administrator, Security Administrator and Global Administrator.

The new View-Only Device Management role is intended to let authorised users inspect device onboarding information without granting them permission to change onboarding configuration or other administrative settings.

The planned read-only capabilities include:

Viewing device onboarding status.

Searching for devices.

Reviewing device configuration details.

Exporting device data.

Existing administrative roles will retain their current level of access, so the change is designed to introduce more choice rather than disrupt established administrative workflows.

You can follow the announcement through Microsoft 365 Roadmap ID 577187.

Why does this matter for Endpoint DLP?

Endpoint DLP depends on supported devices being onboarded and reporting the information needed for monitoring and protection. Administrators need to understand which devices are present, whether they are reporting correctly, and whether their configuration is healthy.

Microsoft’s device onboarding documentation explains how onboarding supports Endpoint DLP and Insider Risk Management, including the monitoring of sensitive information and potentially risky activity on endpoints.

However, not everyone who needs to review this information should be able to change the configuration.

Consider three common scenarios.

1. The security analyst

A security analyst needs to investigate whether a device is onboarded and reporting correctly before troubleshooting a potential DLP issue. They need visibility, not necessarily administrative control.

2. The internal auditor

An auditor needs evidence of device onboarding coverage and may need to export device information for an assurance review. Granting a broad administrative role simply to retrieve that information can create unnecessary privilege.

3. The compliance team

A compliance specialist needs to understand the state of endpoint protection as part of a wider review of data security controls. They should be able to inspect the relevant information without automatically gaining the ability to change onboarding settings.

In each scenario, read-only access is a better fit for the task.

Least privilege is about more than Global Administrator

Organisations rightly focus on reducing the number of Global Administrators. But least privilege is not achieved simply by removing Global Administrator from a few accounts.

It also means examining the everyday administrative tasks that require access to security and compliance platforms.

Ask yourself:

Does this person need to view information, change configuration, or both?

Is the role broader than the task requires?

Can the responsibility be delegated without giving away control of the underlying security settings?

Can access be reviewed and removed when the business need ends?

Roadmap 577187 supports this way of thinking by introducing a more specific access option for device onboarding visibility.

The wider lesson is that read-only access is a security control in its own right. It helps reduce unnecessary privilege while allowing the people responsible for assurance, investigation and reporting to do their jobs.

What should administrators do now?

The feature is listed as In Development, with a preview planned for December 2026 and rollout scheduled to start in January 2027. These are planned dates and may change.

In the meantime, organisations can prepare by reviewing how device onboarding access is currently assigned.

1. Review existing role assignments

Identify who can access the device onboarding area and distinguish between people who administer devices and those who only need to inspect status or export information.

2. Identify opportunities to reduce privilege

Look for auditors, analysts and compliance staff who have been given broad roles solely to obtain device information.

Do not remove existing permissions until you have confirmed that the users’ other responsibilities are covered.

3. Define a read-only access model

Establish which teams need visibility, what information they require, and who should approve and periodically review that access.

4. Validate the new role during preview

When the feature becomes available, test the role in a controlled environment. Confirm the actual permissions, the scope of accessible data, export behaviour and whether any related pages or actions remain restricted.

Do not assume that the role grants access to every device-management function across Purview or Microsoft Defender; validate the documented scope.

The bigger governance picture

This roadmap item may not introduce a new DLP detection capability or change how sensitive data is protected on endpoints. Its value is in how organisations manage access to the controls and information that support those protections.

Effective security governance requires both strong technical controls and appropriate administrative boundaries.

We need people to investigate, review and demonstrate that controls are working. We do not need to give every one of them the ability to change those controls.

The Jim Talks takeaway

The goal is not simply to give fewer people administrator roles. It is to give every person the access they need – and no more than they need.

That is what practical least-privilege governance looks like.

References

Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID 577187

Microsoft Learn: Onboard Windows devices into Microsoft 365

Roadmap status and target dates are based on the published roadmap entry supplied for this article and may change.

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575287: Delegating Copilot DLP Without Giving Away the Keys
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview | Data Loss Prevention | Administrative Units | AI Governance As organisations introduce Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Chat and Copilot Cowork, protecting sensitive information is only part of the challenge. Another question quickly follows: How do you let regional or departmental teams manage their own DLP policies without giving them control over the […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview | Data Loss Prevention | Administrative Units | AI Governance

As organisations introduce Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Chat and Copilot Cowork, protecting sensitive information is only part of the challenge. Another question quickly follows:

How do you let regional or departmental teams manage their own DLP policies without giving them control over the entire tenant?

Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575287 aims to address this by extending Administrative Units support to Data Loss Prevention (DLP) for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Chat and Cowork.

The roadmap currently lists a preview date of October 2026 and General Availability in November 2026. The feature is in development, and release dates may change.

Roadmap details: https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/roadmap?id=575287

What is changing?

Administrative Units (AUs) allow organisations to define administrative boundaries, often aligned to departments, business units or geographical regions.

This roadmap item extends AU support to the management of supported Copilot DLP policies. The intention is to let administrators manage policies within their assigned administrative boundaries without requiring tenant-wide policy-management permissions.

Existing tenant-wide policies continue to apply, and organisations can choose whether to use AU-scoped management.

That distinction matters: this is primarily about delegated administration and policy scope, not a replacement for DLP itself.

Why does this matter?

1. Delegation without tenant-wide control

Imagine a multinational organisation with separate teams responsible for the UK, Europe and North America.

Each team may need to manage DLP policies relevant to its users and regulatory obligations. Giving every regional administrator unrestricted control over all Copilot DLP policies creates unnecessary risk.

Administrative Units offer a way to delegate supported policy-management responsibilities while maintaining clearer boundaries.

2. More practical AI governance

Microsoft Purview DLP can help organisations control how Copilot experiences process sensitive prompts, files and emails, depending on the configured policy and supported scenario.

As Copilot usage expands, governance teams need to consider both the protection controls and who is authorised to manage them.

A regional team might understand its local regulatory requirements better than a central team. Delegation can help bring that expertise into policy management without automatically granting access to the whole tenant.

3. Separation of duties

Good governance is not just about what a policy does. It is also about who can create, change and oversee it.

Scoping administrative responsibilities can reduce the number of people who need broad permissions, support clearer accountability and make ownership easier to define.

However, Administrative Units do not remove the need for role assignments, change control, monitoring or central oversight.

What should organisations do now?

I’d prepare in five areas:

1. Map your administrative boundaries. Identify the departments, regions or business units that need delegated responsibility. Check that your Entra Administrative Units reflect your intended operating model.

2. Review existing Copilot DLP policies. Document the policies already in place, their scope, conditions, actions and owners. Identify which responsibilities genuinely need to be delegated.

3. Define roles and responsibilities. Agree who can create, edit and review policies, who handles incidents, and which changes require central approval.

4. Plan a controlled pilot. When the capability is available in your tenant, test the experience with a small group of restricted administrators. Validate policy scope, permissions, visibility of alerts and activity, and the interaction with existing tenant-wide policies.

5. Keep central governance in place. Establish standards for naming, documentation, testing, exceptions and periodic reviews. Delegated administration should operate within a common governance framework.

The Jim Talks takeaway

AI governance at scale cannot depend on giving every administrator unrestricted control-or forcing every decision through one central team.

The goal is to find the right balance between local accountability and organisation-wide consistency.

Roadmap 575287 is worth watching because it could help organisations delegate Copilot DLP policy management more deliberately, while retaining existing tenant-wide controls.

Give teams the scope they need, keep permissions proportionate, and make sure every delegated policy operates within a clear governance framework.

References

  • Microsoft 365 Roadmap 575287: https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/roadmap?id=575287
  • Microsoft Learn – DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Chat and Cowork: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/dlp-microsoft365-copilot-location-learn-about
  • Microsoft Learn – Administrative Units in Microsoft Purview: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/purview-admin-units

#MicrosoftPurview #Microsoft365Copilot #CopilotCowork #DataLossPrevention #IdentityGovernance #AIGovernance #GovernanceJim

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575285: Extending Network DLP Beyond Known Cloud Apps
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview | Data Loss Prevention | Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access How do you protect sensitive information when users upload it to a website your organisation hasn’t explicitly identified or sanctioned? It’s a challenge for information security teams. Organisations can build detailed Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies for known cloud applications, but users can […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview | Data Loss Prevention | Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access

How do you protect sensitive information when users upload it to a website your organisation hasn’t explicitly identified or sanctioned?

It’s a challenge for information security teams. Organisations can build detailed Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies for known cloud applications, but users can interact with a much wider range of websites, file-sharing services and AI tools.

Microsoft Purview Roadmap 575285 aims to address part of that challenge by extending the scoping options for network data security DLP policies integrated with Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access (GSA) Internet Access.

What is changing?

The roadmap describes a capability that will let administrators scope Purview network data security DLP policies to:

  • All websites.
  • All websites except specific cloud apps.

The stated goal is to extend protection to cloud apps and websites that aren’t listed in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps catalog.

The roadmap currently lists the feature as In development, with preview planned for November 2026 and General Availability planned for December 2026. These dates are estimates and may change.

Roadmap details: https://message.cengizyilmaz.net/roadmap/rm575285-microsoft-purview-data-loss-preventionapply-purview-network-data-security-dlp-policies-to-all-websites-or-all-websites-except-specific-cloud-apps-through-entra-gsa-internet-access-integration

Why does this matter?

1. Less reliance on known application lists

Traditional governance approaches often start by identifying the cloud applications an organisation uses and creating policies around them.

But the web is much larger than an organisation’s approved application list. Employees may use unfamiliar services, new AI tools or websites that have never been assessed by IT.

Broader policy scoping offers another way to address this coverage gap, rather than relying entirely on a list of known destinations.

2. Extending protection to the network layer

Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access provides identity-aware controls for internet traffic. Combined with Microsoft Purview, network data security can inspect supported content and apply DLP decisions as information moves towards web destinations.

Depending on the configured policy and supported scenario, organisations can audit or block content based on sensitive information, sensitivity labels and other supported conditions.

This matters because protection shouldn’t stop at the boundary of Microsoft 365. Sensitive information can leave through browsers, applications, APIs and other routes to external services.

Microsoft Learn: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/global-secure-access/how-to-network-content-filtering

3. A stronger approach to unsanctioned AI and cloud services

Generative AI and file-sharing services introduce additional destinations for sensitive information. Users may have legitimate reasons to work with external services, but that doesn’t mean every upload should be permitted.

Broader DLP policy scope can help organisations apply protection to destinations beyond those explicitly catalogued, while still designing exceptions where business requirements justify them.

The objective isn’t necessarily to block everything. It’s to make decisions about sensitive data movement deliberate, consistent and enforceable.

What should governance teams do now?

I’d use the lead time to prepare in five areas:

1. Review existing DLP policies. Understand which sensitive information types, sensitivity labels, activities and actions are already configured for network data security.

2. Map your current coverage. Identify which cloud apps and web destinations are protected today, where policies depend on known application lists, and where gaps may exist.

3. Define your exception strategy. If you consider an “all websites except specific cloud apps” approach, establish who can approve exceptions, how they are documented and how frequently they are reviewed.

4. Coordinate Purview and Entra teams. Network routing, identity-based policy scope and DLP enforcement need to work together. Review the relevant prerequisites, licensing, traffic forwarding and policy configuration in the Microsoft documentation.

5. Pilot before enforcing broadly. Test representative users, websites, file types and sensitive content. Start with audit and validation where appropriate, then introduce blocking deliberately. Check business workflows, false positives, alerts and user impact.

A governance point worth remembering

Broader scope does not automatically mean complete protection. The capability still depends on supported traffic, inspection scenarios, correct configuration and policies that reflect the organisation’s requirements.

It’s also important to distinguish network data security DLP from basic web filtering. They are related controls, but they don’t perform the same job: inspecting sensitive content and applying a Purview DLP decision is different from allowing or blocking a destination based on a web-filtering rule.

The bigger picture

Data protection needs to follow the information, not just the application.

As cloud services and AI tools continue to multiply, organisations need a practical way to protect sensitive data even when the destination isn’t on a familiar list.

Roadmap 575285 is worth watching because it could give governance teams more flexibility in how they scope network DLP protection.

The Jim Talks takeaway

Don’t build your DLP strategy around the assumption that you already know every destination your users will send data to. Build it around the sensitivity of the information, the risks of the activity and the controls you can reliably enforce.

Roadmap dates and functionality are subject to change. Check the current Microsoft roadmap and Learn documentation before making deployment decisions.
